# Kubernetes TLS Secret fixture provenance (HG-044)

Every manifest in this directory is either a **real `kubectl create secret tls
--dry-run=client` document** or a recorded, mechanical transformation of one,
and every certificate and private key was generated by **real OpenSSL
tooling**. Nothing here is a hand-written byte template.

These are disposable test artifacts. **No production certificate, private key,
hostname, cluster, namespace, or Secret is present.** Every subject and SAN
uses the reserved `.invalid` TLD, and the manifests carry only the test-only
canaries listed below. HarvestGuard's runtime HG-044 detector never invokes
`kubectl`, `helm`, `kustomize`, `openssl`, or any other external process, never
reads a kubeconfig, never opens a network connection, and never writes a
decoded Secret value anywhere: all validation is in-memory against the manifest
bytes the scanner already read.

`--dry-run=client` is purely local. It renders the object `kubectl` *would*
submit and exits; no API server is contacted and no cluster is required or was
available.

## Generation environment

- **OS / container:** Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS (`ubuntu-24.04` GitHub Actions runner
  image), x86-64
- **kubectl:** `v1.36.3` (client version; Kustomize `v5.8.1`), used only with
  `--dry-run=client`
- **Kubernetes object semantics:** `v1` `Secret`, `type: kubernetes.io/tls`
- **OpenSSL:** `OpenSSL 3.0.13 30 Jan 2024` — the key/certificate generation
  tool, used at fixture build time only
- **PyYAML:** 6.0.3 (the declared floor, `PyYAML>=6.0.3`, HG-044 parses with at
  runtime)
- **cryptography:** 50.0.0 (same library and floor, `cryptography>=41.0.0`,
  HG-044 parses certificates and private keys with at runtime)

## Canaries

Seeded so a privacy regression is detectable rather than merely asserted absent:

| Canary | Where it lives |
| --- | --- |
| `hg044-rsa.example.invalid` | RSA certificate Subject CN and SAN |
| `hg044-ec.example.invalid` | ECDSA certificate Subject CN and SAN |
| `hg044-ed25519.example.invalid` | Ed25519 certificate Subject CN and SAN |
| `hg044-other.example.invalid` | Non-matching-pair certificate Subject CN and SAN |
| `hg044-ca.example.invalid` | Chain-position certificate Subject CN |
| `hg044-canary-namespace` | `metadata.namespace` in `rsa_stringdata_secret.yaml` |
| `HG044-CANARY-LABEL` | `metadata.labels` in `rsa_stringdata_secret.yaml` |
| `HG044-CANARY-ANNOTATION` | `metadata.annotations` in `rsa_stringdata_secret.yaml` |

Further canaries (`hg044-canary-name`, `HG044-CANARY-UNRELATED-VALUE`,
`HG044-CANARY-STRINGDATA`, `HG044-CANARY-SECRET`) are seeded by manifests
`tests/test_kubernetes_tls_secret_detection.py` builds at test time from this
same real material.

## Key and certificate generation

All four key pairs are self-signed X.509 certificates with a matching
unencrypted PKCS#8 private key:

```sh
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout rsa.key -out rsa.crt \
  -days 3650 -subj "/CN=hg044-rsa.example.invalid" \
  -addext "subjectAltName=DNS:hg044-rsa.example.invalid"

openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout other.key -out other.crt \
  -days 3650 -subj "/CN=hg044-other.example.invalid" \
  -addext "subjectAltName=DNS:hg044-other.example.invalid"

openssl req -x509 -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:prime256v1 -nodes \
  -keyout ec.key -out ec.crt -days 3650 \
  -subj "/CN=hg044-ec.example.invalid" \
  -addext "subjectAltName=DNS:hg044-ec.example.invalid"

openssl req -x509 -newkey ed25519 -nodes -keyout ed25519.key -out ed25519.crt \
  -days 3650 -subj "/CN=hg044-ed25519.example.invalid" \
  -addext "subjectAltName=DNS:hg044-ed25519.example.invalid"

openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout ca.key -out ca.crt \
  -days 3650 -subj "/CN=hg044-ca.example.invalid"
```

`ca.key` is a build intermediate and is **not committed**: only `ca.crt` is,
and only so a multi-certificate `tls.crt` chain has a second, structurally
valid certificate to carry. HG-044 never builds or validates a chain — `ca.crt`
is not a trust anchor for anything and signs nothing here.

### Container-format conversions

The three accepted private-key PEM labels all need coverage. `PRIVATE KEY`
(PKCS#8) is what OpenSSL wrote above; the other two are re-encodings of the
*same* real key material:

```sh
openssl rsa -in rsa.key -traditional -out rsa_pkcs1.key   # -----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
openssl ec  -in ec.key                -out ec_sec1.key    # -----BEGIN EC PRIVATE KEY-----
```

## Manifests written directly by kubectl

```sh
kubectl create secret tls hg044-rsa --cert=rsa.crt --key=rsa.key \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml  > rsa_data_secret.yaml
kubectl create secret tls hg044-rsa --cert=rsa.crt --key=rsa.key \
  --dry-run=client -o json  > rsa_data_secret.json
kubectl create secret tls hg044-ec --cert=ec.crt --key=ec.key \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml  > ec_data_secret.yaml
kubectl create secret tls hg044-ed25519 --cert=ed25519.crt --key=ed25519.key \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml  > ed25519_data_secret.yaml

cat rsa.crt ca.crt > chain.crt
kubectl create secret tls hg044-chain --cert=chain.crt --key=rsa.key \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml  > multi_cert_secret.yaml
```

`chain.crt` is a build intermediate and is not committed; the chain it produced
lives inside `multi_cert_secret.yaml`'s `tls.crt` value.

## Transformed manifests

`kubectl create secret tls` only ever emits base64 `data`, and it validates the
certificate/key pair, so the `stringData`, mixed-source, precedence, mismatch,
multi-document, and adversarial fixtures cannot come from it directly. Each is
a mechanical transformation of the material above, applied with a short Python
script at build time. The transformation is recorded here per fixture; the
certificate and key bytes are unchanged real OpenSSL output in every case.

| Fixture | Transformation |
| --- | --- |
| `rsa_stringdata_secret.yaml` | `data` replaced by `stringData`, both PEM values inlined as YAML literal block scalars (`\|`); canary namespace, label, and annotation added to `metadata` |
| `rsa_mixed_secret.yaml` | `tls.crt` kept in `data` (base64), `tls.key` moved to `stringData` as a literal block scalar |
| `rsa_override_secret.yaml` | `data` carries `tls.crt` (RSA) and the **non-matching** `other.key`; `stringData` carries the matching `rsa.key`. Only Kubernetes' `stringData`-wins precedence makes this a match |
| `mismatched_secret.yaml` | `rsa.crt` paired with `other.key`, both base64 in `data` |
| `multi_document.yaml` | Four YAML documents in source order: a `ConfigMap` that mentions all three gate tokens in a comment-like value, an empty document, the RSA TLS Secret, and the ECDSA TLS Secret |
| `duplicate_key_secret.yaml` | RSA `data` Secret with `tls.key` present **twice**, the second copy being `other.key` |
| `anchor_alias_secret.yaml` | RSA `data` Secret whose `tls.crt` is a YAML alias (`*crt`) to a top-level anchor (`&crt`) |
| `explicit_tag_secret.yaml` | RSA `data` Secret whose `data` mapping carries an explicit `!!map` tag |

The last three are negative controls: HG-044 rejects the complete YAML file for
each, so no finding is produced from any document in them.

## Private-material warning

The `.key` files and the `tls.key` values inside the manifests are **real,
unencrypted private keys**. They are disposable, were generated solely for this
test suite, protect nothing, and must never be reused anywhere. HarvestGuard
parses them password-less and in-process for a structural check and a
public-key comparison; it never decrypts anything, never prompts for or accepts
a password, never reads a password environment variable, never writes a decoded
value to disk or to a temporary file, and never reports any part of them.
